utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My last question to you today will be to ask you to explain to us in greater detail how the communications were jammed. utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday in examination-in-chief I said that the radio system of the ministry, which existed not only in the territory of Kosovo but also in the territory of the entire Serbia, because Kosovo did not have any special systems that would differ from systems existing elsewhere in Serbia. So these systems were analogue systems, and in such a system of radio networks it was very easy to listen in on those communications and to jam them because the equipment of the Ministry of the Interior and their radio stations did not have any particular encryption, it did not have any special protection. It could be easily wire-tapped and jammed by those who wanted to do that. How did they jam these communications? A lot of radio stations were confiscated by members of the KLA who took radios from MUP members who were killed or wounded. So that's how they got hold of these radios. Then, in addition to that, there were a lot of our colleagues, Albanians, who left the Ministry of the Interior and they were well familiar with the frequencies and how they were set up, these radio links of the ministry. So it wasn't a major technical problem for them to disclose this information. And as for jamming itself, it was very easy to jam. For example, one radio station could block the entire channel, and this is how they would do it. And they would also use various verbal provocations to try to prompt the other side to reply so that the channels of the ministry, before and especially during the bombing, were constantly jammed. In addition, there was also jamming on the part of the international organisations which were in Kosovo. I know this because when radios were confiscated from members of the police they would come to us to see what radio channels had been programmed, and very often those would be the channels that MUP used in Kosovo and Metohija. utterances.text: I would now read a short summary for the Court from this witness's previous statements, and after that I have a few questions for the witness. The witness Hysni Berisha is a Muslim male who has lived in Suva Reka all of his life. The witness describes the events in the Suva Reka after the OSCE evacuated on the 20th of March, 1999. He heard gun-fire and could see flames coming from houses near the technical school on Restane road. He states that on the morning of the 26th of March, 1999, Serb forces started to shell Suva Reka town from tanks and Pragas that had been on the hills behind the town since August 1998. The witness saw a lot of police moving towards the house across from the police station. About two or three hours later, he heard shooting from the police station in the vicinity of Sedat Berisha's house, and he saw smoke and flames coming from that direction. The following day, on seeing the police continue to torch buildings and houses, the witness took his family to the home of a neighbour where there were 70 to 100 people hiding in the basement. They remained there until the early hours of the following morning when they, after this, went to another house until Serb paramilitaries drew closer. After this, they went to a field where they were surrounded by paramilitaries who demanded money and valuables from them. One of these grabbed the witness's daughter and threatened to shoot her unless the witness handed money over. The commander intervened and released the witness's child, telling the witness to go to Albania with his family. The civilians set off in convoy. They were stopped for two days and nights near Korisa, where the civilians in the column were again robbed by paramilitaries of approximately 4.000 Deutschemarks before being allowed to continue to Prizren. En route, a number of civilians were wounded and killed by Serb forces. On the outskirts of Prizren, the convoy was told to return to the places of origin. When the witness arrived back to Suva Reka, his hometown, he saw buildings burning and his home had been looted. Over the ensuing days, he observed numerous Serb forces in military and OSCE vehicles around the whole town, and they were looting shops and homes. He also observed a column of approximately 50.000 civilians passing through Suva Reka. The witness remained in Suva Reka until 10th of May, 1999, when he was again ordered by Serb forces to leave Kosovo. He went to Prizren and stayed at a relative's home until KFOR arrived. The witness followed then KFOR into Suva Reka town. Thereafter, the witness undertook an investigation into the Berisha family massacre and the events at the coffee shop in Suva Reka. He describes the location of items of clothing and artefacts at the murder scenes, victims' homes, and at the cemetery. He also produces a number of documents relating to his investigation. The witness also undertook investigations into other events during March-June 1999, where Kosovar Albanians of Suva Reka municipality were killed, expelled, and their properties looted and burnt. The witness assisted the British forensic team in August 1999 with the exhumation of bodies at the VJ firing range in Korisa, Suva Reka, Prizren firing range. The witness took part in identifying clothes belonging to several victims in Schedule D in the indictment of the Prosecution. The witness is an eye-witness to deportation, looting, and burning in Suva Reka, and he describes perpetrators' uniforms and weapons. He also describes vehicles used and kept account of these vehicles. Thank you.

utterances.text: The British forensic team worked twice at this place, in July 1999 and at the end of August 1999. I went to visit this place without the British forensic team in June -- oh, sorry, in July, while I went there with the British forensic team by the end of August or the 1st of September, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And what happened the 1st of September, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 1st of September, 1999, the whole forensic team of the United Kingdom took their equipment and began exhuming the mass graves. That day, the opening of two mass graves began.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And how many mass graves would it be in total in this range, in this area?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There were two mass graves there which were exhumed on that day. Mass grave 1 and mass grave 2, that's what they were called by the forensic team.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If the witness could be assisted with a pen. And I would like him to draw circles around the places where he is describing these mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If you, Mr. Berisha, please could draw a circle around this mass grave number 1 and mass grave number 2 and just place number 1 and 2 inside the circles so the Court would know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Then I would like put up previous 65 ter number 00122 which would be P00593 in the e-court. And if we could please have page 5 and 6 up on the screen at the same time -- um, before I do this I would like to -- but this is already tendered -- oh, sorry. Yes, if I could please tender this annotated picture. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00597, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And then if I could have 65 ter 00122, which will be P00593. Thank you. And then page 5 and 6 on the screen at the same time. 5 and 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Would you please describe to the Court, Mr. Berisha, what you are seeing on these pictures, the picture to the right is just a detailed or zoomed-in version of the picture to the left.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: This picture reminds me of the worst moment I experienced in September -- on September 1st, 1999. In that mass grave this photograph was found. This is mother and son. This is Zelihe Berisha, my cousin's wife, Hamdi's wife, and her son Mirat. Maybe you cannot see it here or discern what it is, but this is the pencil box, Mirat's pencil box who was in first grade. And that day, it was the first day of school, and on that day he was not amongst us anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you so much --

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: And on not only these two, but seven members of the family were killed. Murat's father, four sisters, mother, and nobody remains from that family.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: The next exhibit I would like to ask for is 65 ter 02351 and that will be P00595, Your Honours. If I can just get that up on the screen. If we can go directly to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for this to come up I can ask you right away, Mr. Berisha, is it correct in 2001 you provided a list to the Office of the Prosecution containing approximately 500 names of deceased people?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: We see the end of this list here of 14 pages. Could you just please describe to us who are these people mentioned in this list, where are they from, and who are they?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: These are victims who were civilians from the villages of the Suhareke municipality and the city itself who were killed by the Serb police and military forces in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the handwriting we can see here on the end of the list, would that be your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. This is the second list after the one that I gave in 2001. That list was corrected and names were added because the list of 2001 had about 500 names. Then the list was amended to have -- to include the names of the people who laid down their lives in the fighting. Later on, people who were killed in Suhareke but were not from Suhareke were taken out of this list and included in other lists. These lists were compiled after the identification of people, bodies, and clothes and artefacts found in various places.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And if we can get up page, I think it might be 5, number 5, it should start with 105, 106. I think it will be page number 4. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Would there be any KLA soldiers in this list, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Allow me to put on my glasses, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Could you please mention which names these would be that were KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. Number 106, Lulzim Shaip Guta; and under 107, Bahri Hajrush Gollopeni, these people are martyrs; and also Naser Hazir Kelmendi, under number 110; while Shpejtim Tafil Kryeziu, under 105, he was not a martyr but a civilian; as well as Naser Hazir Kelmendi, he was also a civilian, meaning that three of them were members of the KLA who were killed and whose names sneaked in on this list, because at that time I did not investigate how these people had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. As you were the author of this list, Mr. Berisha, is this the correct and updated version of this list of the persons who were killed and missing in Suva Reka in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I am the author of this list that I compiled by collecting information on the ground myself from the people who had lost their loved ones and who came to me at the mass grave site where I was with the British and German forensic teams. They came to me, and I took notes of what they said to me on the spot. And this list, that does not include only March 1999 but also April, May, June. There were victims all the time from the time that NATO bombing started.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. But my question was whether this was the updated and so far the correct version of this list of missing persons that you have provided.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the updated list compared to the 2001 list, and I am the author of the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, Mr. Berisha: In your statement you have several times mentioned police, paramilitary, and militaries. Would you explain to the Court how you could distinguish between these units, how would you describe them, how would you describe the uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I have to say that the Serb police and army forces included other units as well. To my opinion, the paramilitaries - maybe I'm wrong - but I considered paramilitaries all those citizens who were mobilised into the police and army forces, the Yugoslav forces. I also considered paramilitaries, because at the time I did not know what kinds of units there were, the special Yugoslav police forces, which at the time were deployed in Suhareke coming from all the towns in Serbia, such as the 137th unit from Nis. And I, at the time, did not know that they were special forces; but because their uniforms were different from the regular army, I considered them paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And how would you describe a regular police uniform, police that you were talking about in your statement?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The regular police had two types of uniforms. One of them was blue, standard, normal blue; the other one was camouflage blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Exactly. And did they have any insignia that you could -- that was visible to you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Usually they had inscriptions on the arm, but also different insignia and signs that distinguished them from other units. They had colours, white and red, that I saw in Suhareke. They had ribbons, white and red ribbons that I saw in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the paramilitaries and the military, how would you describe their uniforms, were there any difference between them; and in that case what?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In this case there were no differences in uniforms, but they differed as far as their outer appearance is concerned. They were unshaven or they had shaven heads. They did not wear caps but had bandannas on their heads. And because of all these things, the tattoos and everything, I thought that they were not regular forces. But some of them were part of the special units that operated in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean to tender the list?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: The list is already tendered, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which exhibit number is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit Number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that P595?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same, and since there is no annotation on it, it will be exactly the same. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Berisha. I will put some questions to you. There won't be great many of them, but they will pertain to certain facts which I as Defence counsel in this case believe need to be clarified. Mr. Berisha, please tell me, before the beginning of the NATO bombing were there any conflicts between the KLA and the Serbian forces in the vicinity of Suva Reka? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know to which period you're referring, 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was quite specific. Before the beginning of NATO bombing, and the NATO bombing began on the 24th of March, 1999; so before that, were there any conflicts between the KLA and the Serbian forces in the vicinity of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In the summer of 1998, that is to say in August and September 1998, the Serb police and military forces launched an offensive in the direction of the western part of Suhareke, i.e., in the direction of Reshtan, Decan, Semetisht, and Nishor villages, where they burned houses, expelled the civilian population, and there were casualties, victims. At the same time, there was another offensive in the direction of Reqan, Malan, and Budakove villages. In this offensive, more than 16 villages were burned down. This was the first offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, if you can, please focus on the questions I'm putting to you. So please give me brief answers. Were there any conflicts between the KLA forces and the Serbian forces in the vicinity of Suva Reka just before the NATO bombing in 1999 and -- in 1998 and early 1999. I didn't ask you anything about civilians, were civilians injured, involved, and so on. I just asked you about any clashes between the KLA and the Serbian forces in the vicinity of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I already stated that in the western part of Suhareke an offensive was launched by the Serb police and military forces. In March 1999, on the 22nd of March, that is, immediately upon the withdrawal of the OSCE observers, there was a clash in the centre of Suhareke. During this clash, a Serb was killed and 11 Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to hold. Again, you are not focusing on the relevant time. Let me phrase it this way: Did the KLA exist in 1998 in the vicinity of Suva Reka or not?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The KLA existed in 1998 in the vicinity of Suhareke but not in Suhareke proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask that. Thank you. My next question: The offensive that you are mentioning, the offensive of the Serbian forces in 1998, am I right in saying that you were referring to the offensive of the Serbian forces against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the offensive of the Serbian forces against a civilian population and civilian facilities, not against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude that the civilians fought against Serbian forces, since you say that it was a -- an offensive against the civilians not against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know how a civilian population can fight police and military forces when this civilian population consisted of women, children, elderly, people who lived in their own homes, and these homes were shelled indiscriminately. The civilian population did not fight. I never heard of a child fighting a police or military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate this with you. My next question: Do you know anything about the killings of the police members regardless of their ethnic background before the NATO bombing, that is to say before the 24th of March, 1999? Do you know of any policemen being killed by the KLA members?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't have such information because I didn't belong to those services that knew these -- about these things. And I didn't read about this either in the media, in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the NATO bombing, were you aware of any cases where some Serbs were kidnapped by the KLA members and later on killed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware about this at the time because nobody told me about this at the time. I heard about such a case at a conference held in Belgrade. I heard about it from family members there, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the killings of the well-known and prominent Serbs in Suva Reka after the beginning of NATO bombing, that is to say after the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Are you referring to civilians or to policemen and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now about the prominent Serb citizens, civilians.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In March 1999 it was impossible for us to know who was killed because we could not move freely at that time. We could hardly leave our houses, so it was impossible for us to have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question deals with the period after the beginning of the NATO bombing. Do you know anything about policemen or members of the army being killed, those who were in the territory of Suva Reka at that time?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this. I don't have any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in the territory of Suva Reka municipality there are 42 villages?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, out of those 42 villages, immediately after the beginning of NATO bombing how much of the territory was under the control of the KLA? I'm now referring to these villages.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the KLA to know which villages were under their control. I can only speak about Suhareke and surrounding villages where there was no KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm asking you. I'm asking you about the vicinity of Suva Reka, the area around it. But do you still know -- do you know nevertheless what units of the KLA were located in the territory of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, would you be so kind and tell me after NATO bombing began, that is to say from the 24th of March, 1999, onwards, what uniforms did you see in the territory around Suva Reka? I'm now referring to the uniforms worn by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I saw police and military uniforms. The -- from police uniforms I saw the camouflage ones, blue camouflage ones, whereas from army uniforms I saw the uniforms worn by the special police units that were operating at the time. And these camouflage uniforms were replaced by green camouflage uniforms, the NATO green. I also saw camouflage uniforms and members of Territorial Defence units wearing both camouflage uniforms and classic uniforms known, during the time that I completed my military service, as the SMB uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well that you said that the special units later on changed their uniforms into green camouflage uniforms? You said that today just a few seconds earlier.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. On the 3rd of April, 1999, when the police forces entered Suhareke, torching everything on their way and coming closer to the location where I was sheltering with other families, around 5.000 people, these forces were wearing blue camouflage uniforms. And I had the opportunity, since one of these policemen took my daughter out of the car and placed her behind a wall, ready to execute her unless I paid him money, this policeman took 50 Deutschemarks from me and the other asked for 1.000 Deutschemarks to release her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I will have to stop you. That wasn't my question. You gave a brief reply to my question by saying that the Serbian special forces changed their uniforms from blue into green. My next question is: How come you know that those were special units? How come you know that to begin with?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: From the policeman himself, he introduced himself as the commander. He said they were from Nis, and he addressed his colleague. He told him to release my daughter. He himself told me that he was coming from Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And that fact alone was sufficient for you to conclude that those were special units?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That is true. There was no reason for me not to believe in what he said. He said himself he was from there, and considering the trial held in Belgrade, you know very well that the statements of the accused relating to the special units operating in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. Berisha, and I'm putting questions to you in this case, in this trial. My next question: How do you know that they changed their uniforms from blue into green ones?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, 1999, large forces with all sorts of vehicles, jeeps, vehicles that I don't know to this date, came to Suhareke from the direction of Dulje. My house is on the side of the road that links Prishtina with Prizren. I counted 106 different types of vehicles, armoured vehicles. They entered the neighbourhood where my house was. They came to my courtyard. These forces were wearing green camouflage uniforms, and this is why I said that they had their uniforms replaced. These were special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's time for a technical break, and I shall continue with my cross after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now have the first break, and we'll resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, we shall continue where we stopped before the break when we discussed the special forces from Nis. If you look at your statement - and I will shortly tell you which specific statement that is - it's the one dated the 20th of August, 2001, and it was given in Kosovo. If you go to page 3, you are describing the incidents when you were asked to give 50 German marks, if you don't do that your daughter would be killed, then the commander appeared telling you he was from Nis. This is all in paragraph 2 on page 3 of your statement. And somewhere in the middle of the second paragraph it reads as follows: "Everybody stopped and members of the paramilitary units went from one vehicle to another ..." and so on and so forth. Mr. Berisha, can you tell me were those members of paramilitary units or were they members of special forces?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: For me they were members of the special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that I mentioned just now, why did you describe them as members of paramilitary units? And you obviously changed your statement today. You said that you carefully reviewed and read your statement. Why this discrepancy now?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I will repeat again that at the time I thought that the regular police and army forces differ from paramilitary units and special units. At the time, I didn't know how this worked; I was not familiar with this organisational structure, which ones were member of regular police or army forces, which ones were members of paramilitary forces. However, these forces were wearing blue police camouflage uniforms. They had black caps, some of them had tattoos, and you judge for yourselves what they were, whether they were regular forces, special forces, or paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's much, much more clear. Mr. Berisha, you mentioned the trial in Belgrade when we discussed our previous topic. What I wanted to ask you now is: Do you have this knowledge from the trial being held in Belgrade or did you acquire your information from other sources? I really don't know why you mentioned the Belgrade trial at all while we were discussing the uniforms, the special forces, and paramilitary units. What was the reason for that? Is it that all the information you got from the trial in Belgrade or did you get it from elsewhere? Can you please give me a short answer.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As I already stated, I attended this court on the 6th of December, 2006, as a witness in the proceedings against eight accused in Belgrade, including the commander of the special forces from Nis. There I gave a testimony, and I was cross-examined by your colleagues, by the Defence counsel of these accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you a lawyer by profession now that you mentioned that you were cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I never worked as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I read somewhere in your CV that you represented yourself as a lawyer; is that an error? Am I right in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know about the interpretation or translation you received. By profession I am a lawyer, but I never worked as a lawyer, I never practiced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What were you actually doing before the war?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I worked in the administration of a construction organisation until I was dismissed from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of that company?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Construction and Industrial Enterprise 19th November Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When did you start working in that company and when did you stop working for it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I started working in the 1979/1980, around that year, and I stopped when I was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When were you dismissed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: When the enterprise went bankrupt by the government at the time. I think it was in the year 1989 or 1990. I don't know the exact year, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, we can agree that your employment was terminated because bankruptcy was filed for this company, not because you were sacked for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I didn't terminate my employment. I was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your company ceased to exist, sir. You are a lawyer. By the way, where did you study law and in what year did you graduate from the law school?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I would like to ask for guidance from the Trial Chamber as to is it necessary for me to answer these questions which are out of the context of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate, Mr. Berisha, where you undertook your law studies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Prishtina university, Faculty of Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you'd like to carry on, Mr. Djordjevic, with another topic I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question. I would like to know the year in which he graduated from the Faculty of Law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I graduated in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When your company went into bankruptcy, you remained jobless. What did you do after that? What did you do for living? Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: What I did to survive was that I migrated. Four years in Germany I spent in order to earn money and feed my family, and I always worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In what year did you come back to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I returned to Kosova on the 22nd of December, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return to Kosovo and Metohija, what did you do for living? How did you support yourself?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I had funds that I had saved from my employment in Germany. I also inherited some land from my parents, and I worked on that land.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. Tell me, please, are you aware of the existence of parallel authorities in Kosovo of the Albanian people, including in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know of any other parallel structures than the education and medical structures. I don't know about any government authorities or civil authorities. If you consider education and medicine as parallel structures, then those are the ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to consider anything. I just wanted to ask you what you know about that. Were you personally involved in any of these parallel systems of education and health care, as you said?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have any problems with the Serbian authorities, and by that I mean political persecution or some criminal proceedings instituted against you particularly or primarily on political grounds?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, because I was very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you started recording all these events, as you said you did it of your own free will. Can you please tell me when it all began.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: All the work and activity I conducted for investigating and finding out about war crimes committed by the Yugoslav police and army against the defenceless civilians started on the 13th of June, on the day when in Suhareke the NATO forces entered, they entered Kosova in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, did you inform anyone about your activities in these investigations?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As regards informing someone about my activities, I did not need to inform anyone because it was not an obligation that I had. With regard to finding the truth about the crimes committed, I gave information to everybody, to every organisation that was interested to know about them and to have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you do this on your own, or did you establish a team for that work?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In the beginning, I started to work on my own. On the 13th of June when the citizens began to come back to Kosova, the ones that had been expelled to Albania. I cooperated with every relative who had been affected, families that had been affected, in order to find the truth about victims, how the bodies of victims had been found, and so on. In the beginning, I served as a bridge, as a liaison, between the inhabitants and the forensic teams working on the ground. I communicated directly with them and the relatives authorised me to be their spokesperson because it was impossible for 500 people to -- or more, to speak to them personally. Later on, seeing that there was a lot of demand, much more demand to find the truth, in the year 2000 myself and family members of victims created or established an organisation for aiding the families of victims and missing persons. This organisation still exists, and I am a chairperson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning that you did this voluntarily. How did this develop later on? Was that not voluntarily any longer? If not, how can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: From the beginning to the end, I worked voluntarily. I still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you start receiving any remuneration for your work from this organisation?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Never. I never received any kind of remuneration. As I already mentioned, I started this work voluntarily, and I'm still working voluntarily. For the years I've been working, I have never received any kind of remuneration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... or you said that a certain organisation had been set up within the government of Suva Reka, this is what you exactly said in your statement. I'm asking you about how you organised your investigation work concerning crimes committed in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know whether you did not understand my statement or what. When you are speaking about an organisation for the investigation of war crimes. If you are speaking about the end of June when we started examining the mass graves in Suhareke, at that time we asked for the assistance of KFOR. And KFOR offered assistance for us to be able to examine the mass graves and to secure the area and to be sure whether there were or not any exploding devices. So that's how we proceeded with opening of graves and exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, am I right to say that most of your knowledge relating to the chronicles that you set up regarding the missing persons and the persons killed during 1999 originates from the next of kin of those who were killed or went missing?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, most of them from the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, during examination-in-chief my learned colleague showed you two photographs of a firing range that you described as mass grave 1 and mass grave 2. Were you present when these mass graves were made?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I was personally there, and I also said that it was the worst day in my life because in addition to those two photographs that you saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I'm afraid I have to stop you. That was not my question. My question was: Were you present when these mass graves were made? In other words, when these people were buried in this particular location. I'm not asking you about a later period. I'm asking you whether you were present at the time when people were buried in either of these two mass graves.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I was lucky I was alive and I was not in that group, because if I had been there, I would be in the grave myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge who buried these people and how?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, there is information. The fate of those, bodies from the moment they were executed in Suhareke, they were loaded on trucks, both people who were dead and some who were not, and who were able to escape and come and testify here at this Court about the events. This is one. Second, who exhumed these bodies from there? Both in the Milutinovic and Milosevic trials but even later there was a witness who testified, a witness who had been forced to load the bodies on these trucks -- on these trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was aimed at what you knew about who had buried these people at the execution site. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that, but of course that is a well-known fact. And I'm not here to speak about things that I have not witnessed myself. There are other people who can witness to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know these witnesses, their first and last names, who had eye-witnessed this or just testified about that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that in the year 2000, maybe it was 2001 or 2002, I can't remember exactly, after receiving information from the workers who had been forced to exhume those bodies and load them on the refrigerator truck, we watched a documentary film; and in that documentary, you could see the workers or the witnesses who had been forced to do that dirty job. And the footage gives -- in that footage they give the names of the people who had forced them to do the loading of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about what you have already told us. I asked you something quite different, and it's clear to everybody here I'm not getting any answer from you but I will move on. Sir, you created a chronicle of the destruction of public and civilian facilities in the territory of Suva Reka municipality, the destruction of private buildings, public buildings, and religious sites, and so on?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, please tell me, when compiling this information, was there an expert present with you such as any engineers, architects, and so on?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: First of all, the things I saw with my own eyes I described them as being burnt and destroyed. I visited different places on the ground and saw the destroyed buildings. I also received information from the villages and the municipality structures that had assessed the damage caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who made the assessment?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The financial assessment was not important to me. I was interested to know how many of them had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know with full certainty who destroyed those buildings, the ones that you listed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know what buildings you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Private buildings, public ones, all the ones that you have described.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Well, when you say facilities, buildings, I think of collective buildings; but what I mean are private houses which were burned, stables, cattle, people were expelled from their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: In relation to everything that you compiled, do you have information as to who caused the damage? Do you have information you feel certain about?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I was an eye-witness of the fact that they were burnt and destroyed. I saw who burnt and destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in relation to all the facilities?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Suhareke. If you are asking me about Suhareke, I can say that I was eye-witness to the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to all the facilities described by you? You know the number that is involved.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There is a municipality report about that and about 12.000 houses were destroyed. That is not my report. That's a municipal report and that is a true figure. That is what resulted after they went on the ground, and I received that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, as a resident of Suva Reka, please tell me, after the NATO bombing began where were the members of the army, where were the members of police, and where were members of any paramilitary forces, volunteers, if any at all? Can you please tell me in which facilities they stayed. For example, during the NATO bombing was the army, were the soldiers, stationed in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, sir, there were no barracks in Suhareke. If you're asking me where the Yugoslav Army and police were stationed after the 24th of March, 1999, I will tell you. The Yugoslav Army was near the vineyards during the NATO bombing but also before NATO bombing because their heavy weaponry were stationed there and they were shelling from that area. Part of the Yugoslav Army was also in -- stationed in a place called Biraq. They also had heavy weaponry there. While the police forces were stationed in the police station in Suhareke in Balkan Hotel. They also had their check-points at the crossroads Reshtan-Suhareke-Pecan and other places as well. A little later, they withdrew from the police station and stationed themselves in private homes, Albanian homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, do you know why they withdrew from the police station?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I know that there was no danger to them. I don't know why they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: Do you know that NATO forces bombed the positions of the Serbian army and police that they were aware of, they bombed them from planes?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. There was no bombing in Suhareke by NATO. The police station was never bombed and was not exposed to any danger. The Assembly building was not bombed. The positions of the army and the police in the private homes were not bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, do you know a person named Bislim Zyrapi?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I've heard his name, I know what village he is from, but I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berisha, please tell me, after leaving your house in Suva Reka, were you and your family escorted by police while travelling in the convoy in which you were the entire time or not?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: If you're talking about escorting the convoy, I would like to say that we were expelled, and we were forced to leave in a certain amount of time and go to Albania. And these were policemen that I used to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... my question was: Were you escorted by members of police along the road you were travelling on at the time, throughout the entire time? Would you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: You miscalled me, sir. I'm not Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As for the escort is concerned, if you're referring to the 3rd of April, 1999, at around 15 or 1600 hours we were ordered by the police to leave for Albania. We went up to Malesia e Re in a convoy. The convoy was about 5 kilometres long. There they held us for three days. The police did not allow us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you escorted by police?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: During those two days we were robbed and looted by the police. They robbed me personally. They made people get off their cars and took their cars away --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... let me interrupt you once again. I don't have any time to waste.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm not Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Once again you haven't answered my question. I will do my best to try to focus you. Please tell me, Mr. Berisha, in the convoy which was 5 kilometres long you say that you were deported. Were there any members of the KLA that you were aware of in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I know it was civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, please tell me, did you know that in the vicinity of Suva Reka there were KLA forces?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: What you mean by "vicinity"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity. I'm now referring to these 45 villages, not all of them, but when I say "in the vicinity," I mean the territory of the municipality of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The KLA was active in the territory of the municipality. This is what I stated in my statement and I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, did you ever see a single member of the KLA; and if so, would you tell me whether they had uniforms or not and in general how they were dressed, if you saw any?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to see member of the KLA in 1998 dressed in uniforms. I've also seen them on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Which television?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was on RTS or RTSH.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the KLA in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No. I couldn't tell whether there was a soldier dressed in civilian's clothes or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Suva Reka, were there any members of civilian protection and Territorial Defence who had been organised by the KLA? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: You mean from the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Naturally. I said "organised by the KLA."

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any such organisation, at least not to what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you will be surprised to hear that the Chief of Staff of the KLA, Mr. Zyrapi, stated that there was civilian protection in Suva Reka. Now my next question, and we are approaching the end of this cross-examination, is this: Do you know who Milorad Nisavic is?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And who is he?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I know him as an appearance. Milorad Nisavic was a security -- state security inspector in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Zoran Lazic is?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. I know Zoran and Miki, the two brothers. I know Zoran from earlier, he was the oldest brother, and he lived very close to my parents' house. Secondly, he worked for a long time as a driver in the organisation that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything else about him? Have you said anything else about him, about Zoran Lazic?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I know that he is Lazo's and Vera's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Hysni Berisha is?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There are many Hysni Berishas, but I guess they should know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Halit Berisha is?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He is a relative of mine, member of the organisation that I chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the organisation that you chair?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Shpresimi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could that be translated for me, please. I know that this word stands for something, it means something. I know it's not a name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that in English "Shpresimi" would be hope or hoping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Dr. Boban Vuksanovic is, Bobak?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I knew Dr. Bobak Vuksanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this doctor was president of Suva Reka municipality? Was he a mayor perhaps?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm not sure but I think he was. As I said, I was at the time in Germany, not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Dr. Bobak Vuksanovic?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I heard that sometime in April or May he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: He was killed and buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I saw the announcement of his death on a pole, on a post, it was sometime in April 1999. I moved about in Suhareke, and I saw the announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that he was killed and it wasn't a case of natural death? How come you know that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As I said, I read this announcement that was published and posted in public places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the doctor was killed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That I don't know. I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And since you were not in Germany in 1999, do you know what the doctor did at the time, say in 1998 and 1999, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In 1999, after the commencement of NATO bombing, I saw Dr. Bobak dressed in green camouflage uniform. I don't know what his job exactly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for Mr. Hysni Berisha. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for coming and telling us what you had to say, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Nilsen, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. I have very few questions for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you were asked by my learned colleague whether you were present when the mass graves were made or present at the time when the people were buried in the two mass graves that you have pointed out for us, and your answer was eventually no. I'm referring to page 37 and 38 of the transcript. My question to you is whether you ever did observe any acts to what you would think related to the preparing or creating of these mass graves in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 3rd of April while in the convoy when we were expelled and ordered to go to Albania by the police forces, we were stopped at that part of the road from the police station in Lubishte, in the direction of Suhareke. I was very near these two grave-sites, one on the right side and one on the left side. It was dark, it was raining, and I heard some machinery working, the noise of this equipment, and the lights of these machines on. I saw two excavators working that day, but I wasn't aware of the work they were doing. Later on it was verified that these two excavators were exhuming the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And these equipment and these machines you are referring to, did you see them? Can you just describe them?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It was impossible because it was raining and it was dark, but I could see the headlights, and I could hear the noise of these vehicles; and that's why I came to the conclusion that these were heavy machinery used to dig or to do some work there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And for how long did you observe this work going on?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I could not say because, as I said, it was cold, it was raining, and we always were scared looking after -- looking to find shelter. So I didn't have a watch at the time. Maybe it was 2.00 or 3.00 -- hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And how far away would you approximately say that you were from these construction workers or these machines at the time?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As the crow flies, I would say about 600, 700 metres, 1 kilometre the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you ever speak to anyone who were involved in loading these bodies that you took part in identifying afterwards into these mass graves?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with three workers that were engaged in loading these bodies. They were employers of Higijena Tehnika from Prizren, two Romas and one Albanian. I spoke with them about what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: These three persons told me that on the 3rd of April, 2nd or 3rd of April, they were forced to load the bodies onto the refrigerator truck, that it was police forces that ordered them to do that. They said that the police were digging the bodies, whereas they were forced to load them onto the truck. They also said that they were beaten and that they were not allowed to look on the size and check for the truck. They didn't know to which direction this truck went. And they also said that after they finished the job they were returned to Prizren. They were very distressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember when this conversation took place with these people?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't quite remember, perhaps in July, late July or early August.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And when did they tell you that they had to load these bodies into the graves, and did they tell you that that took place?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: They didn't know the exact date. They only described the weather. They said it was raining, that it was dark, and that it was sometimes in early April. So I reached the conclusion that this should be the date of their loading the bodies onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And you mean -- you mean the same night as you were observing the lights?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, the same night.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questioning for you. The Chamber has your statement and your previous evidence and what you have been able to tell us today. We would like to thank you for coming to The Hague yet again and for the assistance that you have been able to give. You are now, of course, free to return to your normal activities and the court officer will assist you to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think this would be a practical time for the second break --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and we will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Please could you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I am Halit Berisha. I was born on the 5th of August, 1940, Suhareke, Republic of Kosova now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your current occupation, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I am currently a pensioner, but I was a teacher before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where do you live now, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I live in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In August 2001 did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you recently had the opportunity to review this statement?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN

utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, did you testify previously in the trial of Milutinovic et al. in this Tribunal in September 2006?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
