utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will now read the witness's in-court summary. The witness is a Muslim male from Suva Reka. He was the former mayor of Suva Reka and describes his forcible removal from this role in the early 1990s. The witness also describes the events in Suva Reka from the 24th of March, 1999, including the movement of Serb forces in Suva Reka and snipers positioned in the town. On the 26th of March, 1999, around noon, the witness got a call from his brother, Jashar Berisha, telling him that people had been killed at the shopping centre and that the witness and his family should leave. The witness called his brother later in the afternoon and learned from his brother that Sedat, Nexhat, and Bujar Berisha had been killed by the police and their families and that -- my apologies, and that their families had been massacred in the shopping centre in Suva Reka. On the 28th of March, 1999, the witness heard an explosion and saw the minaret of the mosque in Suva Reka destroyed. Later that evening, a Serb policeman who was a neighbour came to the witness's home and told him that he must go to Albania. The witness then left towards Albania. On his way, he met numerous people from various villages around Suva Reka. The witness then subsequently returned to Suva Reka. In late May 1999 the police came once again to the witness's aunt's house, where the witness was staying, and ordered him and his family to leave for Albania. The witness then left with thousands of others towards Albania. Just outside Prizren, the police stopped the witness and others and checked their identification papers. Some of them had their ID documentation confiscated. In the summer of 1999, the witness participated in the identification of personal belongings found during the exhumations of a mass grave located between Prizren and Suva Reka. There he identified part of his brother's leg based on the clothing worn by his brother on the day he was killed. The witness also provided a blood sample for the purposes of DNA identification. The witness subsequently learned that his brother's remains were identified in Batajnica. The witness's brother is Jashar Berisha who is a scheduled victim in Schedule D of the indictment. That is the end of my in-court summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, since the Trial Chamber already has your previous testimony and statements -- and statement before it, I only have a few questions for you. I would like to take you back to the 26th of March, 1999, that is the day the members of the Berisha family were killed in Suva Reka. I have some questions for you about your brother Jashar Berisha. Mr. Berisha, what did your brother work as?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, 1999, my brother was working at the petrol station in Suhareke of -- station of the firm Beopetrol. He worked there for 30 years. That day in the morning, about 8.00 in the morning, he went to work. He also was at work on the 25th from morning until 5.00 in the afternoon. And I told him not to go to work because there was a war going on and I didn't want him to suffer something bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And at that --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: However, he took his lunch with him and some milk and went to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And how old was your brother at that time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: He was born in 1943.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, going back to the 26th of March when your brother left for work at the petrol station on that day, could you tell us what your brother was wearing?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a blue jacket, on the back of which you could see Beopetrol written on it, the name of the company. He was wearing jeans trousers, and the trousers he also had the bottom part of a track suit and he was also wearing long johns with stripes on the side. This is what he was wearing that day when he went to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you remember what colour the bottom part of his track suit was?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: He was wearing blue jeans, under them the track suit trousers were red, and then his underwear, long underwear, white but with some stripes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. After the 26th of March did you see your brother again?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The last time I spoke to him was at 1400 hours from my aunt's telephone, and from that time on we did not see him again. We waited for him to come back home from work at 5.00 p.m. but he didn't show up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When you say you spoke to him at 1400 hours, what day was that or what was the date that you spoke to him at that time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It was the 26th of March because at 12.20 he called me and said, Leave your homes because there is a massacre going on at the shopping centre. And he told me that Sedat and other people had been killed at the shopping centre. So I got my family members together and my neighbour's family together. We left our homes and went towards the river. We were scared that massacres would happen in other parts of the town just like the one at the shopping centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. I'd now like to take you forward in time. In your testimony in Milutinovic you speak about participating in identifying personal belongings that were found in a mass grave between Prizren and Suva Reka. When did you participate in this process?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The artefacts or personal belongings that were identified were found after we returned from Albania. I returned on the 23rd of June. I was expelled on the 21st of May, and on the 24th and 25th of June, at the place called Kroj e Popit, people had been exhumed. And we found some personal belongings of the bodies, and we also found a leg together with the clothing I described earlier. I was together with my wife and Ramadan Haxhiu. We took the things we found and submitted those things to the English mission. They cleaned the belongings and photographed them, everything we had found, jackets, slippers, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Berisha --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: These were found on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like you to look at a document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If I could call up 65 ter 133, page 6 of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you just told us that you participated in an identification process and that you identified some personal belongings. In this document before you, do you recognise any items that belonged to your brother Jashar Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. KRA/1072. This is part of the leg, so KRA/1072.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is the red piece of cloth that is located just above the leg?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It's the track suit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this exhibit into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I should repeat what I just said. It seems already to be part of Exhibit P591.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In which case I will just make the reference to the document Exhibit P591 and not seek to tender it as a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, we just saw on the screen the -- a part of your brother's limb that you found at this exhumation site. What happened to the rest of his body, do you know?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In the forensic office - I did not know this then but I know it now - the forensic office in Prishtina that dealt with the identification of the bodies, these bodies came from Batajnica in Belgrade, and they told me that both arms and legs had been burnt. I was told that he had been fired at his back and his head. He had bullet marks. He was killed on the 26th of March, 1999. When I gave the statement, I did not know these things, but because we are working to find the truth about missing persons and victims, we work closely with the forensic office in Prishtina and they explained to us everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, just to clarify your answer, was the remains of your brother's body subsequently found in Batajnica? Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you provide a blood sample to a forensic team, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. Myself, my brother Ekrem Berisha and my sister Hajziza Binaku.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berisha, I would now like to move on to another topic. In your statement you speak about an event you witnessed on the 28th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber's reference this is at page 3 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you say that you saw a minaret destroyed on that day. Where were you when you heard this explosion?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 28th of March at 11.55 I was in my garden and at that time I heard an explosion. And when I turned to look what had happened, I immediately saw that I could not see the minaret of the mosque. The mosque is only about 250, 300 metres from my house, so you can clearly see -- you could clearly see the minaret. A few minutes later, because my house is very close to the Prizren-Prishtina road, I saw a car of the Serbian army, camouflage colours, green and olive, which was driving towards Prishtina up to a place called Biraq where the Serbian army was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just stop you there for a moment, Mr. Berisha, just a moment. Before we move on to this car that you saw, going back to the minaret being destroyed, did anyone else witness this explosion to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. Seven or eight minutes later - there is a cousin of mine who is married into the Elshani family, they live close to the mosque, and she told me that the minaret had been mined by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter 1807, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, if you could turn your attention to the document that will appear on the screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, this is the mosque in Suhareke, but in this photograph there is no minaret. The minaret was on my right -- on the right side of the picture as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Before I finish, Mr. Berisha, one final question: Did the 28th of March have any religious or special significance for you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was the significance?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. That was Bajram day, which is a Muslim celebration, but that day nobody went to the mosque to pray for fear that some greater massacre would occur. There was nobody at the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Berisha. I have no further questions for you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute while preparing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As Defence counsel of the accused, Mr. Djordjevic, I'm going to ask you a few questions. My first question, Mr. Berisha, for you is the following: Before the beginning of the NATO bombing, were there any clashes between the Kosovo Liberation Army and the Serbian forces in Suva Reka and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: In Suhareke there were never any clashes because the KLA forces were never present in Suhareke. They were in the villages around Suhareke, yes, but never in Suhareke itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the beginning of NATO bombing, were you personally aware of the cases of abduction of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Prior to the NATO bombing there was only one case when a Serb was killed on the 22nd of March, 1999, in a shop in Suhareke. And that day the Serb police in a street which we call the street behind the old post office, they killed 11 persons that had nothing to do with the killing of that Serb citizen. To this day we know nothing about the bodies of these people who were killed by the Serbian police. They are missing. There were no abductions of Serbs in the town of Suhareke. I don't know about elsewhere, but not in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any such instances took place after the NATO bombing started? I'm not referring only to Suva Reka but to the surrounding villages as well.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I lived in Suhareke. There was war going on in the villages around, but I had no knowledge about the fighting going on in the territory of Suhareke municipality. This was fighting between the Serbian police and army forces and the KLA. There were no such fightings or battles in the town of Suhareke itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge about the killings of members of the police regardless of their ethnicities, both before the NATO bombing and during the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The fighting mainly occurred outside the town of Suhareke, and throughout the time before and during the bombing and up until 21st of May I was first in Suhareke; and as of 28th of March I was in the village of Stavrove. So there were no cases of Serbs being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about members of the police, regardless of whether they were Serbs, Albanians, or any other ethnicity. That was my question. Do you know of any such incidents in which the policemen were killed in the area of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge about the killings of prominent Serbs in Suva Reka after the beginning of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know who you're referring to as prominent Serbs. Those who were prominent Serbs from the mayor of Suhareke and other officials in the municipality, they're still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know what territories in the area of Suva Reka were under the control of the KLA? Please try to give me an answer by making reference to a specific region or village. As far as I know, there were 42 villages in the area of Suva Reka municipality.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: In the area of Suhareke municipality on the right side of the road Prishtina-Prizren, you find the villages of Dobrodeljane and Semetisht, and up to Pagarusha there were the liberation army forces, whereas in Musitiste and in Vorane, where there was Serbs, there were forces -- Serb forces there. The Albanian population was expelled on the 2nd of April in Musitiste and Sopi, in Vranishte and Bukosh they were expelled and ordered to go to Albania. So the villages were emptied of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was in control of the village of Belanica?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The village of Bellanice belongs to Malisheve municipality, not to Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether members of the KLA were there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know. I never was in Bellanice or Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer me this: Do you know which specific KLA units were deployed in the area of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know about specific KLA units, but I know of a certain number of Albanians who took up arms to fight the Serb police and military forces. It was impossible for me to leave the house and even cross the road Prishtina-Prizren because there was a large number of policemen in the town and also locals who were wearing military uniforms. So it was impossible for me to cross on to the other side where the forces of the liberation army were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- or for start, did you ever see members of the KLA in the area of Suva Reka; and in connection with that, did you have an occasion to see what kind of uniforms and arms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. After the 28th of March when a large number of citizens were expelled from Suhareke I went to Stavrove and Budakove and there I saw some KLA soldiers. They were at Budakove in the mountains. The uniform they wore was kind of a camouflage uniform; however, many of them didn't have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us briefly what kind of camouflage uniforms and what kind of weapons did the KLA members have?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform, green pattern, and they had different types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were those members of the KLA who didn't have uniforms wearing? What clothes did they have?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Those who didn't have uniforms had some old clothes, normal civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did some of KLA members wear a kind of mixed clothes, partly military/partly civilian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There were not so many dressed like that. Some had some raincoats to protect them from rain, military coats, and otherwise they had civilian clothes underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, now that we're dealing with the KLA, my next question is this: In the territory of Suva Reka, did the KLA organise civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: While you were staying in Suva Reka, members of the Serbian forces had uniforms. My first question is: Did all of them have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I lived in a neighbourhood only a street separated us from Serbian families, Trajkovic, Cvetkovic, and so forth. They -- members of these families who were older than 18 had uniforms; some had police, blue camouflage uniforms; some others had the military, green camouflage uniforms. A citizen was wearing the typical cap with a sign of the old Serbian monarchy. They were all armed with Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now you are talking about those who were local Serbs, residents of Suva Reka. Did a uniform necessarily denote that they belonged to a certain unit or was that not always the case?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We could tell that those who were wearing blue camouflage uniforms belonged to police units, whereas those with green camouflage uniforms belonged to the army. I saw them with my own eyes, because as I said only a street separated our houses and I knew all of them by their names. They had been mobilised, almost all of them who I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do with uniforms. What other uniforms did you see while staying there in Suva Reka in those unfortunate times?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I happened to see only once part of them wearing black uniforms and red and blue head-scarfs. They moved around in Pinzgauers, and whoever they happened to see in the street they would collect them and those people would never be seen again. This was the only time I saw these kind of forces. As I said, it was impossible for me to go out on the main street; and where I lived, behind there, it was impossible for them to enter this area with their vehicle. So I described to you their clothes. They were wearing black clothes, and they had shaven heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your neighbours, the Trajkovic family and the others. I naturally know that they were not the only Serbs in Suva Reka. How many other people, Serbs, did you recognise wearing police or military uniforms? Could you give us an approximate number, people that you personally knew, at least by sight.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I could not give you their number, but for the majority of them we found some documents in the territorial and civil protection. You can say that there was such, not only in Suhareke but in other Serb villages, Leshan, Popovan, and so on. I personally couldn't go to this -- to these villages to verify this, but those in Suhareke, as I said, were mobilised and were dressed in blue camouflage uniforms and green camouflage uniforms. I don't know the -- their exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, were there any instances where you knew, in relation to, say, a Roma person, a Muslim - if not an Albanian - that he was a member of the Serbian forces? I'm now referring to the local residents.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: You mean local residents that belonged to police units? I think there were two or three such persons. There was a Roma person from Leshan village. He was member of a police unit. I cannot recall his name right now. I don't know his name, but I know that he was a member of a police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These mentioned -- these persons that you mentioned were members of the Serbian forces. Do they live in Suva Reka to this day? Is your answer no? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, they do not live in Suhareke. I don't know where they are currently. They are not in Suhareke municipality, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to briefly revisit 1991. In the documents that were provided by the Prosecution we have some material concerning the Socialist Party of Serbia and the letter 1991 where they request that you and some other individuals, who seem to be Albanian, at least judging by their last names, resign. Could you please give an audible answer for the sake of the transcript. Is it yes? Is your answer yes?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see that letter which was provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I do have that letter. The Socialist Party of Serbia, the branch in Suhareke, requested from the Serbian Assembly to issue a decision for removal of myself as the mayor, then Sefer Ljuznica, and some others. We didn't resign but we were removed, we were dismissed, and our constitutional right was violated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: For ease of reference, Your Honours, please, could we have an exhibit number so that I'm able to follow this document that the witness is referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to be efficient, but all right we will wait up. That's P601. Could we please see that document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I did this because my learned friend asked me to do that. You are obviously familiar with this letter, so I won't ask you to read it right now. But the let me ask you this: The reasons given by them in relation to everybody was the support to the Kacanik group and lack of respect for the constitutional system of the Republic of Serbia and so on. And then they propose that you be dismissed. Could you please tell us something about the reasons why they wrote this, whether these reasons were grounded and whether they represented really your activities in Suva Reka at the time, and this is why the Socialist Party of Serbia proposed this at the time.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know the reason why they wrote this letter. We found this letter upon our return from Albania. Secondly, their reason was to take into their own hands the authority and power in Suhareke municipality, the Serbs. They -- I didn't want to work under those discriminatory laws issued by Serb authorities. The structure of the population in Suhareke at the time was 95 per cent Albanian and 5 per cent Serb. There were 2 or 300 Romas. There were no other ethnicities. So they requested this at the Assembly and then the Assembly issued this decision for us to be dismissed from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that -- you say that Serbia had discriminatory laws. Are you referring to the constitution of Serbia or something else, something broader than that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Discriminatory laws which in 1999 were no longer in use by a decision of the administrator of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We're discussing 1991 when this happened to you. We are not dealing with 1999 at the moment. Now let us move away from that time which is not relevant. My next question is this: From that point in time until the beginning of NATO bombing, the 24th of March, 1999, how did you support yourself? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: From 5th of April, because the decision of the Serbian Assembly was issued on the 4th of April, 1991. On the 5th of April, five persons came to my office and brought me this decision and basically expelled me from office. Later on, I was given another decision on me being dismissed from work. The decision stated that I had no right to appeal. So as that moment -- from that moment onwards I lived from my own funds. I was not involved in any other activity except for agricultural activity. I worked on my own land that I had as my property in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we are told that there's a matter that needs to be raised with the Chamber before we finish tonight. Would that be a convenient time to interrupt your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have enough questions for this witness, not much, but enough to warrant me continuing tomorrow. The document that is on the screen, I will not tender it into evidence. It is already in evidence and I do not wish to dwell on this document any longer. I will continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, if I'm not mistaken. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berisha, we must adjourn for the evening shortly, and we continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. We would ask you to return then to complete your evidence. The court officer will assist you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I understand there's a matter you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I wish to announce to the Court that there were two witnesses, the last witnesses on the schedule for this week will not be available to testify at all this week. And therefore, the next witness will be the last witness brought for this week. On Friday, as it were, the way things were moving with the witness, Professor Dunjic left over to come into this week, and also Witness Deretic, that we thought would take a much longer time having regard to how things were going, there was a discussion with the Victims and Witnesses Unit in which it was -- it became plain that the risk of bringing the witnesses here this week when we did not expect them to be reached was too great because this is not a long weekend, really. If they came and they could not be reached then it would be very costly. So -- but as it turned out it seems that we may have had time for them. So I just wanted to advise the Court that they are not here and that is the reason why the last two witnesses are not here. In the circumstances the next witness, Zogaj, would be the last witness for this week. And the second thing that he arrives today, this evening -- or is expected to arrive this evening and therefore would not be available for testimony at all tomorrow. And that is, to some degree, as a result of the change in the scheduling from evening to morning. That is my understanding. So I just wanted to make the Court aware that we will have witnesses, but if -- depending on how long counsel takes with these witnesses we might have time tomorrow and also on Friday where we don't have witnesses because things speeded up very, very significantly yesterday and today -- sorry, I meant Thursday. When I said "Friday," I meant Thursday. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you sit, Mr. Stamp, did you consult with the Chamber's officers before you made arrangements not to bring these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we did not. We saw how the schedule was working and -- on Friday, and on Friday we were told we would have to decide whether or not they would be brought and what the risks were if they were not brought or if they were brought and could not testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The schedule of witnesses, Mr. Stamp, is in the hands of the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- Mr. Stamp. Do you understand. We should have been consulted through our staff. It means that we must fall behind by two witnesses in the programme for this week. We do appreciate, though, that with the long break that follows, we can understand that you would have a care to try and ensure that no witness was part heard. Your enthusiasm in that regard seems to have been a little too strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, can I turn to the witness yet to come, Shefqet Zogaj, did you say he would not be available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He can be made available tomorrow, Your Honours, but he will arrive tonight, and he would need some time to review his statement and his evidence which is pretty substantial. He would need a couple of hours at least to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're really saying you want us to sit just to finish the present witness for a short time tomorrow morning and then to deal with the witness Zogaj on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I don't know -- yes, Your Honour. That is the situation as it is now. One -- I'm sorry. One alternative that had been suggested but this is something I don't know about is whether or not we could take him in the afternoon and not having to have to return on Friday, but that is not something that I am able to manage. It's way out of my bailiwick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, how long would you anticipate being with the present witness, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at least 20 minutes and not more than 50 minutes tomorrow. So is the Chamber considering that we hear both witnesses on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, the Chamber is considering whether we will hear both witnesses tomorrow, Mr. Djordjevic. My next question is: How long do you anticipate being with the witness Zogaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About one hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, I must add, unless there is some substantial additional information once the Prosecution completes their proofing of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the view of the Chamber is that we should hear both witnesses tomorrow. Because of the position in which you find yourself, we will not commence the evidence of the remaining witness, that is Zogaj, until 11.15. We will finish the present witness, break, and then resume at 11.15. That ought to enable what has to be done in the morning to be accomplished and that commencing at 11.15 ought to enable his evidence to be completed in the usual time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. We'll endeavour to fit within that time schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any particular problem with that ?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is the read-back of the evidence, if we'll have sufficient time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may have to start early, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We will -- we will do whatever is necessary to fit within that time schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will adjourn now to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
